label: Mark Twain
description: American writer and humorist whose vernacular fiction, especially Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, became a major reference point for later American prose.

label: Gertrude Stein
description: Writer and salon figure whose prose experiments, literary circle, and mentorship formed part of Hemingway's Paris apprenticeship.

label: Ezra Pound
description: Modernist poet and editor associated with Imagism; a formative literary contact for Hemingway in Paris.

label: Sherwood Anderson
description: American fiction writer and early mentor to Hemingway who encouraged his fiction and helped connect him to literary contacts.

label: Paul Cézanne
description: Post-Impressionist painter whose methods of seeing, structure, and exact visual relation were important to Hemingway's thinking about prose and description.

label: Kansas City Star newsroom and style sheet
description: The newspaper environment in which the young Hemingway worked as a reporter; its style rules emphasized short sentences, vigorous English, immediacy, and restraint in modifiers.

label: Paris expatriate / Lost Generation milieu
description: The post-World War I expatriate literary world of Paris in which Hemingway worked among writers, artists, editors, and publishers while developing his early fiction.

label: Hemingway — A Farewell to Arms
description: Novel of war, love, injury, disillusionment, and flight whose First World War setting draws heavily on Hemingway's ambulance-service experience in Italy.

label: Hemingway — For Whom the Bell Tolls
description: Spanish Civil War novel about an American volunteer, anti-fascist struggle, violence, solidarity, and disillusionment; Hemingway used his reporting experience in Spain as background.

label: Romanticism
description: Late-eighteenth- and early-nineteenth-century movement emphasizing imagination, subjectivity, emotion, rebellion, nature, the sublime, melancholy, and visionary experience.

label: Gothic literary tradition
description: Tradition of terror, ruined or threatening spaces, secrecy, supernatural ambiguity, psychological extremity, and sensational narrative that precedes and informs Poe's fiction.

label: Ann Radcliffe
description: Gothic novelist whose works helped define the aesthetics of terror, suspense, sublime landscape, and supernatural ambiguity inherited by later Gothic writers including Poe.

label: E. T. A. Hoffmann
description: German Romantic writer of fantastic, uncanny, psychologically unstable tales frequently discussed in scholarship on Poe's literary ancestry.

label: Lord Byron
description: Major Romantic poet associated with the defiant, melancholy Byronic hero and a formative influence on Poe's early poetry.

label: John Keats
description: English Romantic poet whose sensuous lyricism and aesthetic concerns belong to the early poetic field that influenced Poe.

label: Percy Bysshe Shelley
description: English Romantic poet admired by Poe; Poe's early verse drew on Shelleyan as well as Byronic and Keatsian models.

label: Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine terror tale
description: Influential magazine tradition of concentrated sensational and terror fiction that provided a formal model Poe repeatedly emulated and transformed.

label: Poe's early bereavement and Allan household
description: Both of Poe's parents died before he was three; he was then raised in John Allan's Richmond household. The graph records this as documented biography without treating it as a simple psychological cause of his fiction.

label: Poe — The Fall of the House of Usher
description: Gothic tale of a decaying house and family, hypersensitivity, doubling, entombment, atmosphere, and psychological-supernatural ambiguity.

label: Poe — The Murders in the Rue Morgue
description: Ratiocination tale featuring C. Auguste Dupin; widely treated as a foundational model for modern detective fiction.

label: Poe — The Raven
description: Narrative poem of bereavement, obsessive repetition, memory, sound, and the intrusion of an enigmatic raven into a midnight study.
